reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the APC tumour suppressor gene, inherited autosomal dominantly, though a substantial minority of cases arise de novo without a prior family history
Classic FAP produces hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas beginning in adolescence, and colorectal cancer is essentially inevitable if the colon is not removed
Prophylactic colectomy is the cornerstone of management, with the surgical option (total proctocolectomy versus colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis) guided by rectal polyp burden and genotype
The retained rectum or ileal pouch and the duodenum require lifelong endoscopic surveillance because adenomas continue to develop
Duodenal and periampullary adenomas are common and represent the leading cause of cancer death after colectomy, so upper gastrointestinal surveillance is essential
Extraintestinal features (Gardner phenotype) include desmoid tumours, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, dental anomalies, and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
Desmoid tumours, often triggered by surgery, can be locally aggressive and are a major source of morbidity
Attenuated FAP presents with fewer polyps and later-onset cancer, and biallelic MUTYH variants cause a clinically overlapping recessive polyposis
reference.pathophysiology: APC is a tumour suppressor that regulates the Wnt signalling pathway by promoting degradation of beta-catenin. Loss of functional APC allows beta-catenin to accumulate and drive transcription of proliferation genes, initiating adenoma formation throughout the colorectal mucosa. With so many adenomas present, the probability that one will accumulate further mutations and progress to carcinoma approaches certainty over time. APC dysfunction also underlies the extraintestinal manifestations, including the fibroblastic proliferation of desmoid tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis (hamartomatous polyposes)
additionalInvestigations: Germline APC sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, with MUTYH testing if APC is negative
Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy from adolescence to document polyp burden and time surgery
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with a side-viewing duodenoscope for duodenal and periampullary surveillance
Cross-sectional imaging for suspected desmoid disease
Ophthalmological and dental assessment for extraintestinal features where relevant
redFlags: Near-100% lifetime colorectal cancer risk if colectomy is not performed
Advancing duodenal or periampullary adenoma burden signalling risk of upper gastrointestinal cancer
Rapidly enlarging intra-abdominal desmoid causing bowel, ureteric, or vascular compromise
New polyposis in a child or young adult from an affected family who has not yet entered surveillance
reference.prognosis: With timely prophylactic colectomy and structured surveillance, colorectal cancer is largely preventable and life expectancy is greatly improved. Long-term outcome is then dominated by duodenal cancer and desmoid disease, so lifelong upper gastrointestinal and extraintestinal follow-up remains critical.
pitfalls: Deferring or declining colectomy given the near-inevitable colorectal cancer risk
Focusing on the colon and neglecting duodenal and periampullary surveillance
Performing non-essential abdominal surgery that may precipitate desmoid growth
Assuming a negative family history excludes FAP, since de novo APC variants are common
